title: The shape of the Mass
hookLine: gathering, word, table, sending: the Catholic path walks it slowly

lines: BREAD BROKEN, AND THEY KNOW HIM.
cards: Two friends are walking from Jerusalem to a village at the end of a terrible weekend. A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about.

They tell him everything: their teacher, the cross, the empty tomb nobody can explain. And the stranger starts at Moses and walks them through the scriptures, mile after mile. At the village they beg him to stay.
He sits down to eat with them, takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. In that moment they know who he is. The Mass walks a shape much like that road.

teach.b: The Catholic Mass has four movements; the church's own books lay it out that way. First, gathering.

People come in from separate lives: a procession, a song, the sign of the cross, and a moment to admit what's gone wrong this week, answered with Lord, have mercy. Strangers become a congregation. Second, the word.
Readings from the Old Testament, a psalm, a letter, and then everyone stands for the gospel. A homily opens it up.

teach.h: WORD: DID NOT OUR HEART BURN?
teach.b: It's the road to Emmaus again, where the friends said afterward, "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" Third, the table.
Bread and wine are brought forward. The priest prays the great prayer of thanksgiving and repeats the words of Jesus over them, and the people come forward to receive.
Catholics believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.
At Emmaus, "he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him."
Fourth, sending. A blessing, and the people are sent out. The old Latin dismissal says, Ite, missa est.
Roughly, it means go, it is the dismissal, and many hear in it, go, you are sent. Tradition says the word Mass comes from it. The service doesn't so much end as push you out the door.
The friends went the same way: "they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem." Gather, hear, eat, go. Once the four are clear, they turn up in other churches too.

how: Catholics attend Mass on Sundays and holy days; it moves through introductory rites, the Liturgy of the Word, the Liturgy of the Eucharist and the concluding rites, ending with a blessing and a dismissal.

games.q: what does “the shape of the mass” mean?
o: four movements: gathering, word, table and sending
the cross-shaped floor plan of a Catholic church
the order of seats from the altar to the door

games.q: the Mass and the road to Emmaus — tap the pairs.
p: a stranger falls in beside them
he opened to us the scriptures
he took bread, and blessed it
they rose up the same hour

s: the Mass has no set shape; each parish invents its own
the church's books lay it out in four movements: gathering, word, table, sending.
the friends at Emmaus knew Jesus when he broke the bread
"he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened."
the Mass ends by sending people out
a blessing, then the dismissal: go, you are sent.

games.q: you're one of the friends at Emmaus. it's evening, you've just recognized Jesus at the table, and he's vanished. what do you do?
o: get up that same hour and go back to Jerusalem.
keep it to yourselves for now.
games.why: "they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem." the meal sends them straight back down the road.

practice: Walk the four parts slowly: gather, letting the scattered pieces of your day come in and sit down; hear, bringing back one line that's stayed with you this week; the table, remembering the last meal you shared and who sat across from you.
Then go: picture the next place you'll walk into. If you pray, offer each part to God as you go.

wordCard.voice: The shape of the Mass. Four movements: gathering, the word, the table, and sending.

orig.note: Latin: roughly, go, it is the dismissal; many hear in it, go, you are sent. the old dismissal at the end of the Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: gather, hear, eat, go. The road to Emmaus, walked every Sunday. Back tomorrow, same hill.
